title: LEGO Ideas Wallace & Gromit set uses newly developed printed dome eyes
summary: LEGO designers reveal that 21371 Wallace & Gromit required brand new printing technology to create printed 1x1 dome eye pieces, rather than the usual flat printed tiles.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO Ideas 21371 Wallace & Gromit has been officially revealed, and designers Tom Gerardin and Ellen Bowley have shared details of a technical breakthrough behind the set. Speaking in a roundtable interview with Brick Fanatics, the pair explained that the model's eyes aren't reused parts, but the first ever printed small dome elements.

According to the designers, the 1x1 dome piece existed before but wasn't previously printable. The team felt the dome shape was ideal for capturing Wallace and Gromit's famously bulging claymation eyes, so LEGO developed new printing tech specifically to make it possible, rather than falling back on the more common flat printed eye tiles.

Ellen Bowley added that the graphic design team tried numerous approaches to get the print working on the curved element, with a flat-tile version kept as a backup in case it didn't succeed.

## Why it matters
This shows LEGO investing in new manufacturing techniques specifically to nail small details on a licensed Ideas set, rather than settling for existing elements. For fans of buildable figures, character models and printing techniques, it signals a level of craftsmanship that could influence future minifigure and character-based designs.

## What to watch next
It'll be worth watching whether this new printed dome element appears in future LEGO sets beyond Wallace & Gromit, potentially opening up more expressive character builds down the line.

title: LEGO Ideas 21371 Wallace & Gromit revealed - here's how it compares to the fan design

bodyMarkdown:

According to Brick Fanatics, the official set makes heavy use of macaroni elements in new colours to better shape Wallace and Gromit's limbs, giving the figures smoother, more accurate curves than were possible in the fan build. Interestingly, not everything has gone smoother - the sidecar's egg shape now uses sloped and curved pieces rather than an all-curved approach, which reportedly captures the elongated egg shape more faithfully.

The motorbike has also been reworked, with changes to the inner workings and fender to better match its appearance in *A Close Shave*. Wallace and Gromit's minifigure-style heads have been updated too, with more authentic shaping, printed white teeth, and Gromit getting the biggest overhaul - a shorter mouth and a more prominent black nose.

## Why it matters
This is a good example of how a fan-submitted LEGO Ideas project can evolve once LEGO's designers get involved, using techniques and parts that weren't available to the original creator. For UK fans especially, Wallace & Gromit is a beloved homegrown property, so seeing it get official LEGO treatment - and treated well, by the sound of it - is a big deal for collectors and Aardman fans alike.

It launches on 1 October via LEGO Stores and LEGO.com/Star-Wars, priced at £649.99 in the UK (US $799.99 / CAN $1099.99). Anyone who buys within the first 10 days will also receive an exclusive gift-with-purchase: 40897 Darth Vader's Lightsaber, a 174-piece set and the first villain's lightsaber to join LEGO's ongoing lightsaber collection.

## Why it matters
UCS Star Wars sets are among the most sought-after in the hobby, and claiming the "longest LEGO set ever" title is a big deal for collectors and display builders alike. It's also a fresh benchmark for anyone building large-scale MOCs or comparing shelf space requirements — this one will need a serious stretch of display real estate.

## What to watch next
Expect plenty of unboxing videos and build reviews once the set lands on 1 October. Worth watching too whether the early-order lightsaber GWP sells out quickly, and how UK stock levels hold up given the high price point and limited bonus window.
